body.objective: Students will be able to mix colours and build a value scale in paint.
body.iCan: I can mix colours and build a value scale in paint.
successCriteria: I can mix secondary and tertiary colours from primaries
I can build a value scale with tints and shades
I can use complementary or analogous colours on purpose in a composition
body.hook: Painters can make a red apple glow, a sky feel cold or a shadow feel full of colour, all with only a few tubes of paint. The secret isn't buying more colours. It's knowing how to mix them and how to control light and dark.

A hue mixed with black or its complement to make it darker.

study.title: Colour Wheel and Value Studio
study.question: How do painters control colour and value?
study.passage:
Materials: acrylic or tempera paint in red, yellow, blue, white and black; brushes; palette; water; heavy paper.
Part 1, Colour wheel (20 minutes): Paint a 12-part wheel. Start with the primaries (red, yellow, blue), mix the secondaries (orange, green, violet), then the tertiaries (red-orange, yellow-green and so on). Add small amounts of the darker colour to the lighter one.
Part 2, Value scale (15 minutes): Choose one hue. Paint a nine-step scale: four tints (add white), the pure hue, and four shades (add black on one side; on a second strip, darken with the complement instead and compare).
Part 3, Colour schemes (10 minutes): Paint two small thumbnails of the same simple scene (for example a mug on a table): one with a complementary scheme, one with an analogous scheme.
Part 4, Reflect (5 minutes): Which scheme feels calmer? Which feels more energetic? Why?
Tip: Darkening with the complement gives richer shadows than black, which can make colours look muddy.
study.source: Original studio task written for this lesson; colour theory summarized from standard art education sources.

practice.q: What are the three primary colours in painting?
practice.a: Red, yellow and blue.

practice.q: What is a tint?
practice.a: A colour mixed with white.

practice.q: What is a shade?
practice.a: A colour darkened with black or its complement.

practice.q: What does value mean?
practice.a: How light or dark a colour is.

practice.q: What is the complement of red?
practice.a: Green.

practice.q: Mix red and yellow. What secondary do you get?
practice.a: Orange.

practice.q: Name a tertiary colour and how to mix it.
practice.a: Blue-green: mix blue and green (other tertiaries accepted).

practice.q: What is an analogous colour scheme?
practice.a: Three or more colours next to each other on the wheel.

practice.q: Why add dark paint to light paint a little at a time?
practice.a: Dark colours are stronger and quickly overpower the mix.

practice.q: What happens when you mix complements in equal amounts?
practice.a: You get a neutral brown or grey.

practice.q: Why does a value scale matter in painting?
practice.a: Value creates form, depth and contrast.

practice.q: Why might an artist darken with a complement instead of black?
practice.a: It gives richer, more natural shadows; black can make colours muddy.

practice.q: How could colour lead the viewer's eye to a focal point?
practice.a: Put the strongest contrast or a complementary accent at the focal point.

practice.q: Compare the mood of a complementary and an analogous scheme.
practice.a: Complementary feels energetic and high contrast; analogous feels calm and unified.

practice.q: A painting looks flat. Suggest two fixes.
practice.a: Increase the value range, add warm-cool contrast or stronger shadows.

body.objective: Students will be able to use colour schemes.
successCriteria: I can identify monochromatic, analogous, complementary, split-complementary and triadic schemes
I can explain how warm and cool colours affect mood
I can plan an artwork with a chosen scheme
body.hook: Walk into a fast-food restaurant: red and yellow everywhere. Walk into a spa: soft blues and greens. Designers choose colour schemes on purpose because colour changes how we feel before we even notice it.

vocabulary.definition: A planned group of colours used together.
One hue with its tints, tones and shades.
Colours next to each other on the wheel.
Colours opposite each other on the wheel.
Three colours evenly spaced on the wheel.
Reds, oranges and yellows feel warm; blues, greens and violets feel cool.

study.title: Colour and Mood
study.question: How do colour schemes create mood and meaning?
study.passage:
Part 1, Scheme gallery (10 minutes): Look at examples: Picasso's Blue Period (monochromatic blue, sadness), Van Gogh's "Café Terrace at Night" (complementary yellow and blue), a sunset photo (analogous warm). Name each scheme and the mood.
Part 2, Five schemes (20 minutes): Draw one simple line drawing (for example a window with a plant) five times as small thumbnails. Paint or colour each with a different scheme: monochromatic, analogous, complementary, split-complementary (one colour plus the two beside its complement, such as blue with yellow-orange and red-orange), triadic (such as red, yellow, blue).
Part 3, Warm vs cool (10 minutes): Paint the same thumbnail once in warm colours and once in cool. Which feels like morning? Which feels like night?
Part 4, Plan (10 minutes): Choose a mood (calm, tense, joyful, lonely). Choose the scheme that best fits and justify it in two sentences for your final composition next lesson.

body.objective: Students will be able to paint a composition using design principles.
body.iCan: I can paint a composition using design principles.
successCriteria: I can name and identify the principles of design
I can plan a composition with a clear focal point and balance
I can paint a composition that combines colour and design principles
body.hook: Two paintings can use the same colours and still look completely different, because one is organized and the other isn't. The principles of design (balance, emphasis, movement, contrast, unity) are the tools artists use to organize what's on the page.

vocabulary.definition: Ways of organizing elements: balance, contrast, emphasis, movement, pattern, rhythm, unity, proportion.
The area that attracts the eye first.
How visual weight is distributed (symmetrical, asymmetrical, radial).
Dividing the picture into a 3 × 3 grid and placing key elements on the lines or intersections.
The path the viewer's eye takes through a work.
The sense that all parts belong together.

study.title: Putting It Together
study.question: How do design principles organize a painting?
study.passage:
Part 1, Principles hunt (10 minutes): Look at three paintings (for example Hokusai's "The Great Wave," Mary Pratt's still lifes of jelly jars, and a Lawren Harris landscape). For each, find the focal point, the type of balance and how the eye moves.
Part 2, Thumbnails (15 minutes): Using the colour scheme from last lesson, draw four thumbnails of your subject: centred, rule of thirds, diagonal movement, and high-contrast focal point. Choose the strongest.
Part 3, Paint (35 minutes or across classes): Transfer the composition to your final surface. Block in large shapes first, then build up values and details. Keep the strongest contrast and most detail at the focal point. Use repeated colours across the painting for unity.
Part 4, Check (5 minutes): Look from 3 m away. Where does your eye go first? Does it travel through the painting? Make one adjustment.
study.source: Original studio task written for this lesson.
steps: Check from a distance and adjust
discussion: How did placing the subject on a third line change the energy?
Where is your focal point and what makes it stand out?
How did repeating colours create unity?
What did you change after viewing from a distance?
study.product: Complete a painting that uses your chosen colour scheme, a clear focal point and at least three principles of design, with a short statement naming them.

practice.q: What is a focal point?
practice.a: The area the eye sees first.

practice.q: Name three principles of design.
practice.a: Balance, contrast, emphasis, movement, pattern, rhythm, unity, proportion.

practice.q: What is symmetrical balance?
practice.a: Both sides are the same or very similar.

practice.q: What is unity?
practice.a: The sense that all parts belong together.

practice.q: What is the rule of thirds?
practice.a: Placing key elements on a 3 × 3 grid's lines or intersections.

practice.q: What is asymmetrical balance?
practice.a: Different elements with equal visual weight on each side.

practice.q: Name three ways to create emphasis.
practice.a: Contrast, detail, colour, isolation, placement.

practice.q: What is movement in a composition?
practice.a: The path the eye follows.

practice.q: Why block in large shapes first?
practice.a: To set the composition and values before details.

practice.q: Why view a painting from a distance?
practice.a: To see overall composition and value.

practice.q: What is radial balance?
practice.a: Elements radiate from a centre.

practice.q: Why does a bright small area balance a large dull area?
practice.a: Bright colours carry more visual weight.

practice.q: How can diagonals create movement?
practice.a: Diagonal lines lead the eye and feel dynamic.

practice.q: What happens if a painting has two equally strong focal points?
practice.a: The eye is pulled back and forth and the work feels unresolved.

practice.q: How do colour and design principles work together?
practice.a: Colour creates mood while principles organize where the eye goes.

misconceptions: Always placing the subject in the centre
exitTicket: Name your focal point and how you emphasized it.
Name the type of balance in your painting.
